data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a pragmatic, non-inductive rule of action based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), not probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' itself implicitly relies on an inductive assumption that past resistance to falsification correlates with future resistance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' secretly embeds probabilistic expectations about the world.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory necessarily implies believing it is more likely to be true, collapsing the distinction between action and belief.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which remains unproven and improbable) and its epistemic standing after severe testing. A theory that survives severe tests has demonstrated a higher degree of 'verisimilitude'\u2014it has withstood attempts to falsify it where others failed. Choosing it is not an inductive inference that it will hold in the future, but a rational decision to act on the hypothesis that has currently best approximated truth by surviving the most rigorous criticism. The mechanism is 'survival of the fittest' applied to ideas: we prefer the survivor not because we predict its future survival (induction), but because it is the only one currently standing.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
